title: Token and API Authorization Bypass
description: An attacker obtains or forges a mobile-app access token (via credential stuffing, token leakage, session hijacking, or cookie theft) and uses it to issue unauthorized requests to the cloud backend API, potentially commanding vehicle functions without the legitimate user's knowledge.
attack_surface: Cloud API endpoint exposed to mobile clients
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker intercepts or steals a valid OAuth access token from a compromised mobile device or network traffic. 2. Attacker replays the token against the cloud backend API. 3. Backend accepts the token and executes vehicle commands on behalf of the legitimate user.
damage_scenario: Unauthorized vehicle control (lock/unlock, engine start), privacy violation through access to trip history and location data, potential safety hazard if vehicle is commanded while occupied.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general OAuth and mobile-app security practices

title: Malicious OTA Firmware Injection
description: An attacker compromises the OTA delivery pipeline or exploits weak firmware verification to deliver tampered firmware to the TCU or other ECUs, enabling persistent control over vehicle subsystems.
attack_surface: OTA update channel between cloud server and TCU
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker gains access to the OTA distribution server or performs a man-in-the-middle attack on the update channel. 2. Attacker replaces legitimate firmware image with a malicious version. 3. TCU downloads and installs the tampered firmware without detecting the modification.
damage_scenario: Full persistent compromise of the TCU or target ECU, enabling arbitrary code execution, data exfiltration, CAN message injection, and potential safety-critical malfunction.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general automotive OTA security practices

title: Spoofed or Replayed Cloud-to-TCU Commands
description: An attacker captures legitimate cloud-to-TCU command messages and replays them, or crafts spoofed messages that mimic the cloud backend, to trigger unauthorized vehicle actions such as remote unlock or engine start.
attack_surface: Cellular communication channel between cloud backend and TCU
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker captures encrypted or signed command packets from the cloud-to-TCU channel. 2. Attacker replays captured packets or crafts new spoofed commands exploiting weak replay protection. 3. TCU accepts the commands and forwards corresponding CAN messages to vehicle ECUs.
damage_scenario: Unauthorized remote vehicle control, potential safety hazard from unexpected vehicle actions, erosion of user trust in remote-command features.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general replay attack and command-spoofing practices

title: Compromised TCU Injecting CAN Bus Traffic
description: A compromised TCU (via malware, exploit, or physical tampering) injects malicious CAN or Automotive Ethernet frames into the in-vehicle network, potentially controlling safety-critical ECUs such as powertrain or braking systems.
attack_surface: Internal vehicle bus connecting TCU to gateway and ECUs
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises the TCU through a remote exploit or malicious firmware update. 2. Compromised TCU crafts and injects CAN frames targeting specific ECU arbitration IDs. 3. Gateway or destination ECU processes the injected frames as legitimate, executing unintended commands.
damage_scenario: Safety-critical malfunction (unintended acceleration, braking, steering input), vehicle immobilization, cascading failures across interconnected ECUs.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general CAN bus injection research

title: Diagnostic Security-Access Bypass
description: An attacker bypasses the security-access authentication mechanism on the diagnostic interface (OBD-II or proprietary port) to gain elevated access to ECU services, enabling firmware read/write, calibration changes, or safety-system disabling.
attack_surface: OBD-II diagnostic port on the gateway ECU
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker connects a diagnostic tool to the OBD-II port. 2. Attacker exploits weak seed-key algorithms, default credentials, or timing vulnerabilities in the security-access service. 3. Attacker gains elevated diagnostic session and accesses protected services.
damage_scenario: Unauthorized ECU recalibration, firmware extraction or replacement, disabling of safety systems (airbags, ABS), odometer manipulation, theft enablement through immobilizer bypass.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general automotive diagnostic security practices

title: Telemetry and Location Data Exfiltration
description: An attacker intercepts, eavesdrops on, or exfiltrates vehicle telemetry and GPS location data from the TCU-to-cloud channel or from stored data on the cloud backend, compromising driver privacy and enabling physical surveillance or stalking.
attack_surface: Telemetry upload channel and cloud storage APIs
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises the telemetry upload channel (weak TLS, misconfigured endpoints) or gains unauthorized access to cloud telemetry storage. 2. Attacker extracts GPS coordinates, speed profiles, driving patterns, and personal data. 3. Data is used for surveillance, stalking, insurance fraud, or sold on the black market.
damage_scenario: Severe privacy violation, physical safety risk from location tracking, regulatory penalties (GDPR/CCPA), reputational damage to OEM.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general connected-vehicle privacy concerns

title: Firmware Signing Key Compromise
description: An attacker obtains the private key used to sign OTA firmware packages, enabling them to sign arbitrary malicious firmware that passes the vehicle's signature verification and is accepted as legitimate.
attack_surface: OTA build and signing infrastructure
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises the build server, HSM, or key management system holding the firmware signing key. 2. Attacker signs a malicious firmware image with the stolen key. 3. Vehicles accept the firmware as authentic, bypassing all integrity checks.
damage_scenario: Fleet-wide compromise through trusted malicious updates, complete loss of firmware integrity assurance, costly key revocation and re-provisioning across the fleet.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general code-signing and PKI security practices

title: Certificate Authority Impersonation
description: An attacker impersonates or compromises the certificate authority used for TLS or code-signing certificates in the vehicle ecosystem, enabling issuance of fraudulent certificates that are trusted by vehicles and backend systems.
attack_surface: PKI trust chain used by mobile app, cloud, and vehicle
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker compromises an intermediate CA or exploits weak CA validation. 2. Attacker issues fraudulent server or code-signing certificates. 3. Vehicles or mobile apps trust the fraudulent certificates, enabling impersonation of legitimate services.
damage_scenario: Man-in-the-middle attacks on all TLS channels, fraudulent firmware signing, complete erosion of trust infrastructure.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general PKI and certificate security practices

title: OTA Firmware Rollback Attack
description: An attacker forces a vehicle ECU to accept an older firmware version that contains known vulnerabilities, bypassing patches and security fixes previously applied through OTA updates.
attack_surface: OTA update mechanism version-checking logic
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker captures or obtains a legitimately signed but outdated firmware image. 2. Attacker delivers the old firmware to the TCU. 3. TCU accepts the downgrade because anti-rollback protections are absent or bypassable.
damage_scenario: Re-introduction of patched vulnerabilities, enabling exploitation of known bugs, undermining the entire OTA security update process.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general firmware rollback attack techniques

title: TCU Denial-of-Service via Network Flooding
description: An attacker floods the TCU's cellular or network interface with excessive traffic, exhausting processing resources and preventing legitimate communication between the vehicle and cloud backend.
attack_surface: TCU cellular modem and network stack
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker identifies the TCU's cellular IP or sends excessive requests via the cloud interface. 2. Attacker floods the connection with malformed or high-volume packets. 3. TCU becomes unresponsive, dropping legitimate OTA updates, telemetry uploads, and remote commands.
damage_scenario: Loss of remote vehicle management capability, missed critical security updates, inability to send emergency telemetry, degraded user experience.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general network DoS attack techniques

title: Audit and Security Log Tampering
description: An attacker with access to the TCU, gateway, or cloud backend modifies or deletes security and audit logs to conceal evidence of a prior attack, hindering incident response and forensic investigation.
attack_surface: Log storage on TCU, gateway ECU, and cloud backend
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker gains elevated access to a vehicle ECU or cloud server. 2. Attacker locates and modifies or deletes security event logs. 3. Forensic evidence of the initial attack is destroyed, preventing detection and response.
damage_scenario: Loss of forensic evidence, inability to detect ongoing attacks, regulatory non-compliance with logging requirements, undermined incident response capability.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general log integrity and anti-forensics practices

title: Supply-Chain Component Backdoor
description: A malicious actor in the supply chain introduces a hardware or software backdoor into a vehicle ECU or software component during manufacturing, enabling covert remote access or data exfiltration after deployment.
attack_surface: Third-party ECU hardware and software components
threat_scenario: 1. A compromised supplier embeds a backdoor in ECU firmware or hardware during manufacturing. 2. The backdoored component passes standard quality checks and is integrated into vehicles. 3. After deployment, the attacker activates the backdoor remotely or via a trigger condition.
damage_scenario: Undetectable persistent access to vehicle systems, fleet-wide compromise if the same component is used across models, data theft, and potential safety-critical manipulation.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general supply-chain security concerns

title: Bluetooth Diagnostic Adapter Exploitation
description: An attacker exploits vulnerabilities in a Bluetooth diagnostic adapter connected to the vehicle's OBD-II port or gateway, gaining wireless access to diagnostic services and the in-vehicle network without physical contact.
attack_surface: Bluetooth wireless interface of the diagnostic adapter
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker discovers a Bluetooth diagnostic adapter within radio range. 2. Attacker exploits weak pairing, default PINs, or known Bluetooth vulnerabilities to connect. 3. Through the adapter, attacker sends diagnostic commands to the gateway ECU and accesses the in-vehicle network.
damage_scenario: Wireless unauthorized access to diagnostic services, ECU manipulation, potential CAN bus injection through the adapter's gateway connection.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general Bluetooth and OBD adapter security research

title: Wi-Fi Diagnostic Interface Abuse
description: An attacker connects to an open or weakly-protected Wi-Fi diagnostic interface on the vehicle or a connected service tool, gaining unauthorized access to diagnostic services, firmware, or in-vehicle data.
attack_surface: Wi-Fi access point on vehicle or diagnostic tool
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker scans for Wi-Fi networks near the target vehicle and discovers a diagnostic SSID. 2. Attacker connects using default or cracked credentials. 3. Attacker accesses diagnostic services, reads ECU data, or injects commands.
damage_scenario: Unauthorized diagnostic access, data extraction, potential vehicle manipulation through diagnostic services.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general Wi-Fi and diagnostic interface security practices

title: Infotainment System Pivot to Vehicle Network
description: An attacker compromises the infotainment ECU (via USB, Bluetooth, browser exploit, or malicious media file) and uses it as a pivot point to reach safety-critical ECUs through the in-vehicle network.
attack_surface: Infotainment ECU's external-facing interfaces and internal bus connection
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker delivers a malicious payload to the infotainment system via USB, Bluetooth media, or a browser exploit. 2. Payload achieves code execution on the infotainment ECU. 3. From the infotainment ECU, attacker sends CAN frames to the gateway or directly to other ECUs.
damage_scenario: Lateral movement from a low-criticality to high-criticality domain, potential control of safety systems, data exfiltration, persistent presence on the vehicle network.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general automotive infotainment attack research

title: CAN Bus Flooding and Denial of Service
description: An attacker with access to the CAN bus floods it with high-priority frames, preventing legitimate ECU communication and causing functional failures across vehicle systems.
attack_surface: CAN bus accessible through a compromised ECU or physical port
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker gains access to the CAN bus via a compromised ECU, OBD-II port, or aftermarket device. 2. Attacker floods the bus with dominant (high-priority) frames at maximum rate. 3. Legitimate ECU frames are starved due to CAN arbitration, causing communication failures.
damage_scenario: Loss of inter-ECU communication, potential safety system failures (ABS, ESP, airbag), limp-home mode activation, vehicle immobilization.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general CAN bus DoS research

title: Central Gateway Misconfiguration
description: The central gateway ECU is deployed with misconfigured firewall rules, routing tables, or access control policies, allowing unauthorized traffic to flow between network domains that should be isolated.
attack_surface: Gateway ECU routing and filtering configuration
threat_scenario: 1. Gateway is deployed with overly permissive default rules or a configuration error. 2. An attacker or compromised ECU discovers that messages from a low-trust domain are forwarded to a high-trust domain. 3. Attacker exploits the misconfiguration to send commands to safety-critical ECUs.
damage_scenario: Bypass of network segmentation, unauthorized cross-domain communication, potential safety-critical ECU manipulation.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general network gateway misconfiguration risks

title: Mobile App Tampering and Repackaging
description: An attacker reverse-engineers the legitimate mobile companion app, injects malicious code, repackages it, and distributes it through unofficial channels, tricking users into installing it and exposing their credentials and vehicle access.
attack_surface: Mobile app distribution and runtime integrity
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker decompiles the official mobile app and extracts API keys, endpoints, and authentication logic. 2. Attacker modifies the app to capture user credentials or inject unauthorized commands. 3. Repackaged app is distributed via third-party app stores or phishing links.
damage_scenario: Mass credential theft, unauthorized vehicle access for multiple users, reputational damage, potential financial liability for the OEM.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general mobile app security practices

title: Cloud API Rate-Limit Abuse and Denial of Service
description: An attacker sends a high volume of API requests to the cloud backend, overwhelming the service and denying legitimate users and vehicles access to telematics, OTA, and remote-command functions.
attack_surface: Public-facing cloud API endpoints
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker identifies public API endpoints through app reverse-engineering or documentation. 2. Attacker sends a flood of requests from distributed sources, exceeding rate limits or exploiting their absence. 3. Backend services become overloaded, rejecting legitimate requests from vehicles and users.
damage_scenario: Service outage for all connected vehicles, missed OTA updates, inability to send remote commands, degraded customer experience, potential SLA violations.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general API rate-limiting and DDoS mitigation practices

title: OTA Server Infrastructure Compromise
description: An attacker compromises the OTA update server infrastructure (through credential theft, unpatched vulnerabilities, or insider threat), gaining the ability to distribute malicious firmware updates to the entire vehicle fleet.
attack_surface: OTA server admin interfaces, CI/CD pipeline, and deployment infrastructure
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker gains access to OTA server through phished admin credentials or exploiting an unpatched vulnerability. 2. Attacker modifies the firmware repository or build pipeline to inject malicious code. 3. Malicious firmware is distributed to vehicles as a legitimate update.
damage_scenario: Fleet-wide compromise, massive recall potential, irreversible damage if safety systems are affected, catastrophic reputational and financial impact.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general server infrastructure and supply-chain security practices

title: Privacy Over-Collection of Vehicle Telemetry
description: The telematics system collects more personal data than necessary (detailed location history, driving behavior biometrics, in-cabin audio) without adequate consent or purpose limitation, violating privacy regulations and exposing users to surveillance risks.
attack_surface: Telemetry data collection pipeline and cloud storage
threat_scenario: 1. Telematics system is configured to collect granular location, speed, acceleration, and behavioral data. 2. Data is stored without adequate anonymization or retention limits. 3. Data breach or insider access exposes detailed personal profiles of vehicle owners.
damage_scenario: GDPR/CCPA regulatory fines, class-action lawsuits, loss of customer trust, detailed personal profiling enabling stalking or discrimination.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general automotive privacy and data protection concerns

title: Time-Synchronization Manipulation
description: An attacker manipulates the time source used by the TCU or cloud backend, causing certificate validation failures, enabling replay of expired tokens, corrupting log timestamps, or triggering premature/delayed OTA updates.
attack_surface: NTP/time-sync service used by TCU and cloud
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker performs a man-in-the-middle attack on the NTP traffic or compromises the time server. 2. TCU or cloud backend accepts a manipulated time value. 3. Expired certificates appear valid, replay windows are extended, and log timestamps become unreliable.
damage_scenario: Bypass of time-based security controls, extended replay attack windows, corrupted audit trails, potential acceptance of expired or revoked certificates.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general NTP and time-synchronization security practices

title: Man-in-the-Middle on Cloud-to-TCU Channel
description: An attacker intercepts and actively modifies communication between the cloud backend and TCU by exploiting weak TLS configuration, compromised certificates, or rogue base stations, enabling real-time command alteration and data theft. NOTE: This is a deliberate hard negative relative to TP-003. TP-003 focuses on replay/spoofing of captured messages; TP-023 focuses on active real-time interception and modification.
attack_surface: Cellular link between cloud backend and TCU
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker deploys a rogue cellular base station or compromises a network intermediary. 2. Attacker performs TLS downgrade or presents a fraudulent certificate to intercept traffic. 3. Attacker modifies commands in transit (e.g., changing target ECU, altering parameters) before forwarding to the TCU.
damage_scenario: Real-time manipulation of vehicle commands, injection of unauthorized actions, undetectable data theft, complete loss of channel confidentiality and integrity.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern. DELIBERATE HARD NEGATIVE vs TP-003: TP-003 covers replay/spoofing; TP-023 covers active MITM interception. Both target Cloud-TCU channel (TB-02) but use different attack techniques.

title: Insecure OTA Update Metadata Spoofing
description: An attacker spoofs or tampers with OTA update metadata (version numbers, target ECU identifiers, update urgency flags) without altering the firmware payload itself, causing vehicles to misroute updates, skip critical patches, or apply updates to wrong ECUs.
attack_surface: OTA metadata distribution channel and manifest files
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker intercepts or compromises the OTA manifest delivery. 2. Attacker modifies metadata fields: changes target ECU ID, lowers version number, or marks a critical update as optional. 3. Vehicle processes the spoofed metadata, applying the update incorrectly or skipping it entirely.
damage_scenario: Wrong ECU receives an incompatible update causing malfunction, critical security patches are skipped, vehicles remain vulnerable to known exploits.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern. DELIBERATE HARD NEGATIVE vs TP-002, TP-009, and TP-020: TP-024 targets OTA metadata and manifest poisoning without altering firmware payloads, distinct from malicious firmware binary injection (TP-002), version rollback of signed binaries (TP-009), and full OTA server compromise (TP-020).

title: ECU Firmware Extraction and Reverse Engineering
description: An attacker extracts firmware from an ECU using JTAG, debug ports, or glitching attacks, then reverse-engineers it to discover vulnerabilities, extract cryptographic keys, or understand proprietary protocols for use in other attacks.
attack_surface: ECU debug ports and physical access points
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker obtains physical access to a vehicle or a replacement ECU. 2. Attacker uses JTAG/SWD debug interface or fault injection to extract firmware from flash memory. 3. Reverse engineering reveals hardcoded keys, authentication algorithms, or exploitable vulnerabilities.
damage_scenario: Exposure of proprietary algorithms and cryptographic keys, enabling targeted attacks against the entire fleet using the same firmware, intellectual property theft.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general embedded systems reverse engineering practices

title: Insecure Credential Storage on Mobile Device
description: The mobile companion app stores access tokens, API keys, or user credentials insecurely on the mobile device (plaintext shared preferences, unprotected keychain, world-readable files), enabling extraction by malware or physical device access.
attack_surface: Mobile device local storage and app sandbox
threat_scenario: 1. User installs a malicious app or attacker gains physical access to an unlocked device. 2. Attacker extracts stored tokens or credentials from insecure storage locations. 3. Stolen credentials are used to access the cloud API and control the vehicle.
damage_scenario: Account takeover, unauthorized vehicle control, privacy breach through access to trip history and personal data.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern. DELIBERATE HARD NEGATIVE vs TP-018: TP-026 addresses at-rest insecure credential storage in device sandbox/keychain without modifying the app binary, distinct from binary tampering and repackaging in TP-018.

title: Rogue OBD-II Device Injection
description: An attacker installs a rogue device on the OBD-II port that passively sniffs CAN traffic, actively injects malicious frames, or provides covert remote access to the in-vehicle network through a hidden cellular or Bluetooth modem.
attack_surface: Physically accessible OBD-II port
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker or malicious valet plugs a small rogue device into the OBD-II port. 2. Device sniffs CAN traffic and transmits it via hidden cellular/BT modem, or injects pre-programmed CAN frames. 3. Vehicle owner is unaware of the persistent eavesdropping or manipulation capability.
damage_scenario: Persistent covert access to vehicle network, tracking via CAN-derived location, selective CAN frame injection enabling theft or harassment, long-term data exfiltration.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general OBD dongle and aftermarket device security concerns

title: Gateway Firewall Rule Bypass
description: An attacker discovers a way to bypass the central gateway ECU's message-filtering rules through protocol-level tricks, fragmentation, or exploiting rule-ordering flaws, sending unauthorized messages between isolated network domains.
attack_surface: Gateway ECU message filtering and routing engine
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker analyzes the gateway's filtering behavior by sending probe messages from a compromised ECU. 2. Attacker identifies rule gaps, ordering flaws, or protocol-level bypass techniques. 3. Attacker sends crafted messages that pass through the gateway to a restricted domain.
damage_scenario: Cross-domain attack reaching safety-critical ECUs, bypass of the primary network segmentation defense, enabling attacks that gateway was designed to prevent.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general firewall bypass and gateway security testing practices

title: Compromised Cloud Administrator Credential Abuse
description: An attacker obtains cloud administrator credentials through phishing, credential stuffing, or insider collusion, gaining full access to the backend infrastructure including user data, OTA pipeline, and vehicle command interfaces.
attack_surface: Cloud admin portal and management APIs
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker targets cloud administrators with spear-phishing or finds reused credentials in breach databases. 2. Attacker logs in to the admin portal and escalates privileges. 3. Attacker accesses user data, modifies OTA configurations, or issues bulk vehicle commands.
damage_scenario: Complete backend compromise, mass data breach affecting all users, ability to push malicious OTA updates, tampering with audit logs to cover tracks.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern. DELIBERATE HARD NEGATIVE vs TP-020 and TP-001: TP-029 addresses administrative plane credential abuse and insider privilege escalation across multi-tenant fleet management, distinct from specialized OTA server infrastructure compromise (TP-020) and end-user access token bypass (TP-001).

title: Weak Bluetooth Pairing Exploitation
description: An attacker exploits weak Bluetooth pairing mechanisms (legacy pairing, short PINs, Just Works mode) on the vehicle's Bluetooth interface or a connected diagnostic adapter to establish an unauthorized connection and access vehicle services.
attack_surface: Bluetooth pairing interface on vehicle or diagnostic adapter
threat_scenario: 1. Attacker identifies a Bluetooth-enabled vehicle component or adapter using scanning tools. 2. Attacker exploits Just Works pairing, brute-forces a short PIN, or performs a pairing downgrade attack. 3. Once paired, attacker accesses Bluetooth profiles that connect to diagnostic or infotainment services.
damage_scenario: Unauthorized wireless access to vehicle services, potential diagnostic command injection, eavesdropping on Bluetooth audio or data channels.
source_note: Authored synthetic pattern inspired by general Bluetooth security and pairing vulnerability research
